prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep B046 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye. The essential mechanism is simple and general: at the magic wavelength the lattice light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held and interrogated without perturbing the transition. That combines the small systematic shifts of a trapped single ion with the statistics of a large ensemble, and it is the step that made the 1e-18 regime and many-body clock physics reachable. It answers the chair's novelty question: the 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems; a lattice-clock citation recognises ensemble trapping without light-shift error and the accuracy it opened, which neither prize covered. The systematics are understood quantitatively, which matters to me more than raw performance, and independent confirmation at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere, including agreement between different atomic species, shows that the result is understood and reproducible. The two-name credit maps onto concept plus first demonstration (Katori) and record accuracy plus many-body clocks (Ye).
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that this is a third recognition in the precision-frequency chain and that the demonstrated fundamental-physics yield so far consists of limits and demonstrations (redshift over millimetres, bounds on constants and dark matter) rather than discoveries. I take that seriously as a difference of kind from B038, where a new class of matter was predicted and then observed. A second objection is attribution: Lemonde (SYRTE), Takamoto and Ludlow have real contributions, and the exact priority history among them is recalled from memory by all of us and is unchecked. I do not think either objection is decisive: the citation can be worded around the invention, and a two-name prize leaves a visible gap but not a misattribution of the central idea.

responses.point: Kroll corrects the factual premise that Ye shares the 2005 prize: the 2005 laureates were Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and Ye, as Hall's postdoc, was not one of them. He also notes that Katori's proposal and the Takamoto demonstration preceded the Ye group's record work.
responses.response: I accept the correction and withdraw the statement in my round-1 file that Ye already shares the 2005 prize. As I recall it, the 2005 prize went to Glauber, Hall and Hansch, and Ye was Hall's postdoc and not a laureate; the chair should have this settled on the record, but I will not rely on the overlap argument against B046 any more. That removes the part of my reservation that concerned the same person being honoured twice, though not the question of the same chain of work. On priority I agree that Katori's concept came first. I would keep the citation on invention and realization of the lattice clock and would not add Takamoto: the Sr lattice demonstration came from Katori's group, and a third name would invite the Lemonde and Ludlow question without a clear stopping point.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B038 but does not oppose B046; she argues that the clock leans on comb technology for readout, that the priority history is unsettled, and that a clock prize may be stronger after the SI second is redefined.
responses.response: On the comb, the readout dependence is true of every optical clock, so it does not distinguish the lattice invention; what is new is the trapping scheme and the systematics it removes. On timing I disagree gently: the physical result (clocks agreeing at the 1e-18 level across laboratories and species) already exists and does not depend on a metrology-body decision, and tying the prize to that schedule would make the science wait on administration. I do agree with you that the priority question should not be waved away, and that is why I want the citation narrow. Where you press attribution against B038, I think you are right that the gap there (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, and the 3D work) is wider than the gap in B046, and for me that difference in the cleanness of the account decides between two strong candidates.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B038 slightly above B046 because a predicted and then verified new state of matter changes what we understand about materials, and answers the 2016 overlap on conceptual grounds (Z2 class versus Chern number and phase transitions).
responses.response: I find the conceptual distinction from 2016 credible, and I agree that the Z2 classification is a different object from the Hall-plateau topological invariant, so I no longer treat the overlap as a veto. I would disagree on the weight that conceptual novelty should carry here. Kane and Mele and Molenkamp are each defensible, but the HgTe proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang decided where Molenkamp looked, and a citation that says 'prediction and first observation' with a theory half that is not the proposal tested leaves a mismatch I cannot resolve from the files. If the condensed-matter members can show that Kane-Mele and the HgTe experiment stand without the proposal, I would give B038 real weight; I have put it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Danielsson regards B046 as the strongest alternative to his B038, but says much of the achievement is engineering of known atomic physics, and that the discoveries enabled so far are demonstrations rather than findings.
responses.response: I partly agree: the findings enabled so far are limits and demonstrations, and I do not want to oversell them. But I would not call the lattice clock the engineering of known atomic physics. The magic-wavelength condition is a conceptual step about how to cancel a perturbation while keeping the system trapped, and its consequence, quantitatively understood systematics at the 1e-18 level, is itself a measurement of nature that no earlier scheme could make, as the millimetre-scale redshift comparison shows. Metrology of this kind is what you call patient work that nature rewards, and I would accept your own phrase as the standard. I disagree that it ranks below a new-matter prediction on rigour; the difference is in kind, and the committee's rule counts invention as well as discovery.

uncertainties: The 2005 prize facts (Glauber, Hall, Hansch; Ye not a laureate) are recalled from memory and agreed by one colleague; the committee should confirm them from the Academy's records before the overlap argument is used either way.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow have claims strong enough to add to or displace Katori and Ye; priority details are unchecked recollection.
Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or as continuation of the same line.
Whether B038 can be given a defensible citation without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which would change my ordering of the two leaders.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I am at the University of Gothenburg, in the same physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson at Chalmers, with no collaboration with them or with Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp that I am aware of. My own earlier first choice, B036, is no longer in my configuration.
